analysis.one_liner: Delays federal rules cutting toxic air pollution from coal-fired power plants by two to four years.
analysis.headline: The bill to postpone coal-plant air pollution deadlines was referred to the Senate environment committee the day it was introduced and never received a vote before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have pushed back the deadlines in two 2011 EPA rules: the standards requiring power plants to cut mercury and other hazardous air pollutants, and the cross-state rule requiring cuts in sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides that blow across state lines. It would have added at least two years to the hazardous-pollution compliance deadline and pushed the cross-state reductions to January 2015 and January 2017. In exchange, plant owners would have had to file implementation plans, reviewed by the national Electric Reliability Organization and the Energy Department, spelling out when each plant would retire or install controls.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of coal- and oil-fired power plants, particularly the older units that would have needed expensive new pollution controls or early retirement, would have gained two to four more years without those costs. The coal mining industry also benefits from keeping plants burning coal longer.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal-fired power plant owners and coal miners

how_it_helps.text: Extends the compliance deadline for hazardous air pollutant standards (the proposed Utility MACT rule) by at least two years beyond the standard three-year compliance period, expressly overriding the Clean Air Act schedule otherwise required.

Delays the cross-state air pollution rule so states could not be required to implement first-phase sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide reductions before January 1, 2015, or second-phase reductions before January 1, 2017.

Creates a formal reliability review: plant owners submit draft plans to the Electric Reliability Organization, and the Energy Secretary issues a final plan within 60 days, letting operators build grid-reliability concerns into their compliance schedules.

analysis.who_pays: People living downwind of coal-fired plants would breathe mercury, fine particulates, and smog-forming pollution for the added years; the underlying rules were projected to prevent premature deaths and developmental harm from mercury, so delay carries real health costs. Ratepayers would eventually still pay for the controls, just later.

drawbacks.text: Delaying the rules lengthens public exposure to mercury, a neurotoxin that harms fetal and child development, and to fine particulate matter and ozone precursors linked to heart and lung disease.

The bill would have overridden compliance schedules set under the Clean Air Act's ordinary three-year timeline, even though EPA rules already allowed case-by-case extensions of up to two years for grid reliability; the bill instead delayed deadlines industry-wide.

The good-faith objection supporters would acknowledge: retrofit schedules for large plants are genuinely tight, unplanned retirements can strain the grid, and compliance costs would flow into electricity bills, which is why the bill paired delays with a formal reliability review process.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is cash-flow relief for utilities over a few years, while its cost is additional years of mercury and soot exposure for people living downwind of coal plants. The reliability-review provisions addressed a real concern, but the underlying EPA rules already permitted extensions for reliability problems, so the broad, automatic delay traded public health for utility cost avoidance without a matching public benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced and never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Joe Manchin introduced the bill on November 9, 2011, joined by Senators Coats, Nelson of Nebraska, and Corker, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
Eight senators cosponsored the bill: six Republicans and two Democrats.

The bill would have extended the compliance deadline for hazardous air pollutant standards from electric utility steam generating units by at least two additional years, and delayed state implementation of cross-state sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide reductions to no earlier than January 2015 and January 2017.
The bill contained savings clauses stating that it did not modify the underlying emissions reduction requirements, only their timing.
No further action was ever recorded: the bill sat in committee with no hearings, markup, or vote recorded before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died in committee, the EPA's hazardous air pollutant standards and cross-state pollution rule were not delayed by it, so residents downwind of coal plants, and especially children exposed to mercury, are better off than they would have been had it passed. Coal-plant operators did not get the compliance extension they sought.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan: a Democratic sponsor and eight cosponsors split six Republicans and two Democrats, but the Democratic-controlled committee never advanced the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have given plant owners two to four extra years before having to install mercury, sulfur dioxide, and nitrogen oxide controls, deferring major capital costs. The cost lands on people breathing the pollution during the delay years.

Delaying compliance deadlines slows plant retirements and control retrofits, keeping coal plants burning coal longer and sustaining demand for mined coal. The public cost is prolonged emissions from coal generation.
A two-to-four-year delay pushes back orders for scrubbers, mercury control systems, and related retrofit work. In this case their interest ran with faster cleanup, which also serves public health.
